item.title: Bahrain takes Iran to the UN after Saturday's strike; tankers still burning in Hormuz
item.description:
Bahrain demanded United Nations Security Council action and compensation from Iran on Sunday, a day after an Iranian missile-and-drone attack on US positions in the kingdom set fire to a civilian industrial facility — and Reuters now reports two people were hurt in that fire, one of them critically. The US says its forces and equipment were not affected. Meanwhile the tanker the attack sequence left burning in the Strait of Hormuz is still at anchor, and Iran announced rolling power cuts starting Sunday.
The attack itself was covered in last night's brief: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit two US Patriot radars at the al-Riffa and Awali Sakhir air bases in retaliation for alleged US drone violations of Iranian airspace, while Bahrain said its defences intercepted a number of incoming attacks. What's new this morning is the fallout. Bahrain's Foreign Ministry said on Sunday it is demanding action by the UN Security Council and compensation from Iran, according to a developing report, and Reuters reports the industrial-site fire injured two people — a Pakistani resident in critical condition and a Bahraini citizen in stable condition — revising last night's preliminary account of no injuries. A US official separately told CBS News the latest Iranian attack attempts had not affected American forces or military assets, and the US military has still not commented publicly. The Saudi-led coalition also intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile early on Sunday headed toward western Saudi Arabia, and Iran's navy again claimed a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine in a restricted area — an account Reuters could not verify or link to the reported incidents.
At sea, the picture is settling but not resolved. Two tankers were struck near Oman's Khasab on Saturday — one on the stern about 11 nautical miles north, the second in its engine room 17 nautical miles east — and a navigational warning has now named one of them, the TORKEL, as burning at anchor. No casualties were reported in either strike and the environmental impact is still unknown. No new tanker attacks were reported on Sunday. Iran's navy says a ship hit a mine; the UK maritime agency says the vessels were hit by unknown projectiles, and the two accounts have not been reconciled. Tehran also confirmed a Qatari mediation delegation visited Iran for talks, and Iran's deputy foreign minister repeated that its proposal for a two-day ceasefire and reopening of the strait is still on the table. Separately, the head of Iran's national electricity company told state television the country will be forced into rolling power cuts starting Sunday.
The two sides are still talking past each other. Tehran frames its strikes as retaliation for airspace violations and calls the US blockade of its oil exports an act of war, saying it will take every necessary step to break it. Bahrain's Defence Force called the attacks a "systematic hostile approach" and its Interior Ministry called the strike "heinous Iranian aggression." Washington's public line remains minimal — no damage to US forces, no comment from the military — which leaves open whether the US treats Saturday as a one-off retaliation or the start of a new round. Iran, for its part, is publicly keeping a diplomatic door open through Qatar while its military keeps hitting Gulf targets.
For people in the region, the cost is now showing up in daily life on both sides of the Gulf: another night of sirens and shelter warnings in Bahrain, two people in hospital, and rolling power cuts in Iran as its grid strains under sanctions and war. For everyone else, the shipping war keeps the risk premium on oil intact — Brent was trading around $90–92 a barrel — and every tanker hit near Hormuz is another reason fuel prices stay jumpy.
In short: Bahrain is taking Iran to the UN Security Council over Saturday's strike, which injured two people at a civilian industrial site; the US says its forces were unaffected, Qatar is mediating in Tehran, and the TORKEL is still burning at anchor in the strait — with Iran now announcing rolling power cuts at home.
Sources:
Source: headlinesxtra.com.

item.title: Russian drones collapse a Kyiv-region apartment block; a week of strikes totals 2,700 drones
item.description:
A Russian drone struck a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, about 45 km north of Kyiv, on Sunday morning, collapsing part of the building from the first floor to the fifth. At least 14 people are unaccounted for and may be trapped under the rubble, President Zelenskyy said, and one body had been recovered by Sunday morning. Nine residents, including a child, were evacuated, and two people, including a teenager, were injured. It was the sharpest single incident in another heavy overnight attack — Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 186 drones, 161 of which were shot down, with hits at 18 locations.
The overnight barrage caps a brutal week. Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russian forces launched around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, at 20 regions across Ukraine during the week. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces struck port infrastructure at Kiliia in the Odesa region, the 330-kV Pravoberezhna electrical substation in Zaporizhzhia, and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea northeast of Odesa that it alleged was carrying dual-use goods for the Ukrainian military. Ukraine also kept hitting back inside Russia: Belgorod region's governor said the region came under 138 attacks in 24 hours, leaving one person dead and six injured, and Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences intercepted 170 Ukrainian drones overnight over several Russian regions and the Black and Azov seas.
Kyiv and Moscow are describing the same week in opposite terms. Zelenskyy says Russia is deliberately escalating strikes on energy infrastructure to pressure Ukraine's position ahead of talks, and has repeatedly pointed to the low interception rate on ballistic missiles and the strain on air defences. Moscow says it is striking military-industrial facilities, energy sites and transport infrastructure that supply Ukraine's armed forces, and presents its own air defences as intercepting the bulk of Ukrainian drones. Neither side's claims about interception rates or targets can be independently verified in full, and both sides' casualty and damage figures come from their own officials.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the week has meant another round of emergency outages, damaged homes and rescue crews digging through rubble on a Sunday morning. Dymer is a small town, not a front-line city — the strike hit a residential entrance, and the search for the 14 missing was still going on as the brief was written. Power generation and substations were hit in nine regions in earlier attacks this week, and emergency outages remain in force in Kyiv and several other regions. In Russia's Belgorod region, civilians are likewise living under daily attack warnings, with one person killed and six injured in the past day.
In short: a Russian drone collapsed part of an apartment building north of Kyiv on Sunday morning, leaving 14 people unaccounted for, capping a week in which Zelenskyy says Russia fired about 2,700 drones and 165 missiles at 20 regions — while Ukraine kept striking back into Russia's border regions.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Sparta II still burning off Finland; sinking risk now the worry
item.description:
The fire aboard the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, hit by two drones on Saturday in the Gulf of Finland, burned through the night and into Sunday, Reuters reports.
Finnish, Estonian and Russian vessels are still spraying the ship with water cannons under Finnish command, and by midday Sunday the visible flames had subsided but the cargo stayed hot. The Finnish Border Guard warned the water being pumped aboard risks destabilising the hull — the ship has developed a slight list and sinking cannot be ruled out.
The plan is for Russian rescue vessels to tow it out of Finnish waters once conditions permit. No oil has been reported entering the sea.
Finland's military still says Ukraine was likely behind the strike; Kyiv has not commented. Estonia's navy commander said further attacks in the Gulf of Finland cannot be ruled out.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Poland/NATO — Council meets Monday; no Article 4 invoked
item.description:
NATO's North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels on Monday to discuss Friday's violation of Polish airspace by two suspected Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone, with Poland represented by Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski.
New details: a Swedish Gripen pilot patrolling Polish airspace received NATO authorisation to shoot down the suspected Kh-101 cruise missile but held fire because severe weather prevented visual confirmation, and Poland has not formally invoked Article 4 — Warsaw instead requested extra NATO assets and allied consultations. Polish authorities also warned on Sunday of Russian disinformation around unverified reports of a drone attack on the Kaliningrad exclave; Lithuania rejected allegations its territory or airspace was used for any such attack, and Moscow has not commented on Friday's incursion.

Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Google's Gemini can now control Mac computers and perform tasks
item.description:
Google rolled out "computer use" in the Gemini app for Mac on Thursday, November 19, Bloomberg reports: the assistant can click, type, navigate menus and fill in forms across desktop apps, local files and websites, working in the background while the user keeps control of the screen.
It stops for logins and payments and needs confirmation for sensitive actions. For now it is US-only, English-only, for paying subscribers on Google AI Plus, Pro or Ultra plans, on Apple silicon Macs running macOS Sequoia 15 or later — no Windows version or expansion timeline announced.
It matters because it moves Gemini from answering questions to doing work on a personal computer, and it raises the pressure on Apple to make Siri more capable. Catch-up item — the launch was Thursday and was missed by Friday's briefs.

item.title: Ruby Ships Fixes for 7 Flaws, Including Critical Ruby2Shell, Said to Hit Default Rails Apps Pre-Auth
item.description:
Ruby released fixes on November 18 for seven memory-safety flaws in its regex engine and string case-conversion code.
The worst, CVE-2026-132825 ("Ruby2Shell"), is a one-byte heap overflow when Ruby changes the case of a string in single-byte encodings like ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252, and researchers at Veria Labs say it is reachable over the network, without authentication, in default Rails and classic Sinatra apps — Rack changes the case of a request field during normal form processing, so a fresh Rails app hits the flaw before its own code runs. The Ruby team says it is aware of proof-of-concept exploits showing code execution for some of the seven flaws.
Fixed in Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14; no known in-the-wild exploitation yet, and the researchers plan to publish their PoC about a week after disclosure. Self-hosted software that bundles Ruby — GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, Discourse — is also exposed.
Sources:
Source: thehackernews.com.

item.title: USDA cyber incident disrupted farmer payments for a week (catch-up, Nov 19–20)
item.description:
A cybersecurity incident at the US Department of Agriculture took Farm Service Agency loan software and the Natural Resources Conservation Service's ProTracts payment system offline for most of last week.
USDA's security operations centre uncovered the incident on Monday, November 16, and reset all database passwords in all environments, which is what took the applications down. Two former USDA officials told NBC News hackers breached a payment system; USDA has not confirmed a breach, and Under Secretary Richard Fordyce said no personal information was compromised and no data was lost, with most systems expected back by Friday evening.
The disruption hit just as farmers face a December 11 deadline to enrol in 2026 ARC/PLC programmes. Sources:
Source: dtnpf.com.

item.title: Huge Baltic SMS leak exposed 125 million messages (catch-up, Nov 11–12)
item.description:
Cybernews researchers found an unauthenticated ClickHouse database run by CSC Telecom's Latvian branch holding 125 million+ SMS messages from October 2022 to September 2026, updating in real time — including one-time login codes, password-reset links, medical test results, and bank alerts with IBANs, amounts and balances from Swedbank and SEB, plus airBaltic flight details and messages from Latvia's 112 emergency line.
The database was found September 28 and closed October 27; CSC Telecom says its preliminary investigation found no data was downloaded, and Cybernews says it has no evidence of malicious access. Swedbank has stopped using the provider and opened an investigation.

Source: cybernews.com.

item.title: F5 BIG-IP emergency patches are out
item.description:
F5 released out-of-band hotfixes on Wednesday, November 18, for six critical (9.8) stack-based buffer overflow flaws in BIG-IP's data plane that let an unauthenticated attacker crash the Traffic Management Microkernel and possibly execute code remotely.
Each flaw needs a specific virtual-server setup (an iRule using a particular command, or an APM policy with two particular agents). No exploitation has been reported and there is no workaround — install the engineering hotfixes.
Follow-up to the November 18 disclosure already covered. Source:
Source: bleepingcomputer.com.

item.title: TfL Oyster photocard breach now confirmed
item.description:
Transport for London has confirmed that details of about 265,000 Oyster photocard holders may have been exposed after suspicious activity was detected on the photocard website on November 16, including names, emails, phone numbers, home addresses, dates of birth and security questions and answers.
Passwords, payment card details and journey information were not affected, TfL says, and the incident has been reported to the Information Commissioner's Office. This corroborates the single-source report from November 18.

item.title: Iran strikes US bases in Bahrain with missiles and drones — first confirmed damage there
item.description:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said late Saturday it launched a combined missile and drone attack on US military positions in Bahrain, and Bahrain confirmed an Iranian attack set fire to a civilian industrial facility — the first time an Iranian strike has caused confirmed damage on Bahraini soil, and a sharp step up after weeks of drone attacks on the island that were all intercepted.
The IRGC said its Aerospace Force targeted the radars of two US Patriot air defence systems at the al-Riffa and Awali Sakhir air bases, and claimed both radars were destroyed. The strike was presented as retaliation for alleged violations of Iranian airspace by two US drones — an MQ-1 Predator and an MQ-9 Reaper — earlier on Saturday; Iranian state broadcaster IRIB released footage it said showed both drones being shot down over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's semi-official Fars news agency had earlier named different targets — the Sheikh Isa and Juffair bases — a discrepancy the IRGC's own statement did not address. Bahrain's Defence Force said its air defences intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks late on Saturday, and the Interior Ministry said the attack hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire that civil defence teams were working to contain, with material damage but no injuries. Air raid sirens sounded across Bahrain and residents were told to move to the nearest safe place. Iranian state media also claimed a US interceptor missile launched from the Fifth Fleet base crashed on Sitra Island and started a large fire — an Iranian claim that has not been independently verified. The US military has not commented on the attack. US Central Command did deny a separate Iranian claim on Friday that a surface-to-air missile had damaged a US F-16.
The two sides are telling very different stories about what happened and why. Tehran says its airspace is a "red line" and that any violation will get a "harsh and decisive" response, and it also cited an attack on a radar installation on Iran's Hengam Island. Bahrain's Interior Ministry called the attack "heinous Iranian aggression." Washington has said nothing yet, which matters because the US has been on the receiving end of Iranian drone attacks on Bahrain before — at least three in recent days after a lull — but those were all intercepted with no damage. This time something got through, or at least something burned on the ground.
The backdrop is the same standoff covered in this evening's brief: President Trump says he will not decide on another round of major strikes on Iran until after the new year, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is pressing for a four-to-seven-day joint air campaign. On Saturday, Vice President JD Vance declined to directly endorse Trump's assertion that Iran had been close to acquiring a nuclear weapon when the war began — a small but public break in the administration's messaging. The Associated Press also reports Iran unveiled a new dual-missile launcher on state television, meant to show its missile programme is intact, and that Qatari mediators remain in contact with both sides.
For people in the Gulf, the attack means another night of sirens and shelter alerts in Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet headquarters, and more uncertainty for the shipping war in the Strait of Hormuz, where three tankers were hit on Saturday. For everyone else, the cost keeps showing up in fuel prices: Brent crude is trading around $90–92 a barrel, with the risk premium intact as long as the strikes keep coming.
In short: Iran hit US positions in Bahrain with missiles and drones on Saturday night, claiming it destroyed two Patriot radars; Bahrain says a civilian facility caught fire and nobody was hurt, and the US has not commented — the first Iranian attack on Bahrain to cause confirmed damage, and a direct test of Trump's decision to wait until January.

Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Russian cargo ship hit by drones in the Gulf of Finland, drifts burning into Finnish waters
item.description:
A Russian cargo ship with links to the military was hit by two drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, drifting into Finnish waters in what Finland said was likely an attack by Ukraine — a new expansion of the war into the Baltic, and the second ship struck in the Gulf of Finland this month.
The Sparta II, a 121-metre Russian-flagged roll-on/roll-off cargo vessel owned by Oboronlogistika — a company that provides logistics for the Russian Defence Ministry and is under US sanctions — was sailing from St. Petersburg to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad when it was struck in international waters west of Russia's Gogland island, about three nautical miles from Russia's maritime border. The ship's 16 crew evacuated onto lifeboats and were picked up by a nearby Russian ship; no injuries were reported. The fire was still burning late on Saturday, and Finland warned it could rage for days or even weeks, with a risk of further explosions that could sink the vessel. Finland is leading the rescue operation, has imposed temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Finland, and sent coast guard units to fight the fire and prepare for pollution. Swedish combat aircraft, operating under Finnish command, took part in safeguarding the area, and Estonia sent a navy vessel to help with firefighting. A Russian helicopter was suspected of briefly violating Finnish airspace during the rescue operation, Finland's coast guard said.
Finland's armed forces said it was likely Ukraine was behind the attack, though it was not clear why this particular ship was targeted, and Ukraine's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "The war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said on X, adding that "Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor." Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote that "the consequences of fighting Russia's aggression have reached the Baltic Sea." The Finnish Border Guard said there was no confirmed information about what cargo was on board, but that military materiel could not be ruled out. Russia has previously described attacks on its commercial vessels outside its territorial waters as terrorism and maritime piracy; its embassy in Helsinki did not immediately respond, and the Kaliningrad governor said the incident posed no threat to supplies to the region. The Institute for the Study of War notes the Sparta II is under US and Ukrainian sanctions as part of Russia's military logistics infrastructure, and Finland's military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area.
For people in the region, the strike brings the war into a narrow shipping lane that carries Russian trade to St. Petersburg and is now watched by two of NATO's newest members — Finland and Sweden joined in 2023 and 2024 — with patrol aircraft and temporary flight restrictions overhead. For shipping, it is another reminder that the Baltic, like the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, is no longer a safe commercial waterway during this war.
In short: two drones hit the sanctioned, military-linked Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday; the crew got off safely, the burning ship drifted into Finnish waters, and Finland says Ukraine was likely behind it — the war's second Baltic ship strike this month.
Sources:
Source: cnn.com.

item.title: Gas pipeline explosion and fire at Iraq's Hartha power station
item.description:
At least four people were killed and 35 injured in a fire at the Hartha power station north of Basra on Saturday morning, Iraqi security officials told Reuters, with the toll expected to rise.
Iraq's Health Ministry put the toll lower, at two dead and 46 injured, while Shafaq News reported eight dead. The fire broke out at around 6 a.m. after a gas pipeline feeding the plant ruptured, spreading to nearby houses and forcing the station — 800 MW installed, running at about 400 MW — to shut down completely.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered an urgent investigation. Officials have not said what caused the pipeline to rupture; video shared on social media prompted claims of a drone attack, but no official has confirmed that, and authorities describe the incident as a gas pipeline explosion.
Sources:
Source: krro.com.

item.title: Rackspace cloud breach exposed customer Kubernetes secrets
item.description:
Rackspace told customers that attackers used leaked credentials on November 17 (about 00:20–22:00 UTC) to access its Rackspace Spot Kubernetes cloud, create pods, read Kubernetes Secrets — which can hold passwords, tokens and API keys — and list nodes and volumes.
The company learned of the intrusion on November 18 after a customer report, revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed unauthorised pods and rotated keys. Service was fully restored on November 21.
Rackspace has not said how many customers were affected or whether data was stolen. Source:

item.title: Houthis now 60 km from Aden as government forces claim counter-gains
item.description:
Houthi fighters have advanced to within about 60 kilometres of Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government, after capturing two districts in neighbouring Lahj province, military and government sources told AFP. The fighters are positioned at Al-Kharaz camp in Al-Madaribah district, one of the two districts — Al-Maqatirah and Al-Madaribah — reported captured. France 24 and Al Jazeera carried the same account, and the Institute for the Study of War's November 21 update records government forces fighting Houthi fighters in northern and central Lahij to stop the advance toward Aden.
The advance is the latest step in a ground campaign that has been moving fast since the civil war reignited this summer. The government has already pulled its last forces back from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait area to defend Aden, and the Houthis have taken over evacuated positions along more than 150 km of Red Sea coastline, from Dhubab toward Khor Amira. According to sources cited by the Institute for the Study of War, the Houthis are now building fortifications — tunnels and berms — along Bab al-Mandeb to develop a long-term ability to threaten civilian shipping in the strait at close range, exploiting the vacuum left by the government's withdrawal from all positions within 65 km of the strait. Inside Aden, the government has been digging trenches, building earth barricades and setting up checkpoints, and Yemen's parliament has unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a terrorist organisation.
The picture is not one-sided, though the claims cut both ways and neither side's battlefield reporting can be independently verified. An independent Yemeni journalist reported on Saturday that government-aligned forces assaulted and recaptured several Houthi-held positions near Am Sarih, north of Jabal Kharaz mountain in central Lahij, and retook Jabal Habanan, about 15 km north of Am Sarih — but the Institute for the Study of War says it cannot verify any of those claims. Yemen's army said on Monday it had carried out 661 attacks on Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as part of its "Dawn of Yemen" offensive launched October 5. The Houthis, for their part, say they are only hitting military and strategic targets; Riyadh calls them a terrorist militia deliberately targeting civilians.
For people in Aden, the war is now a question of distance measured in tens of kilometres, with missiles already falling on the city and the forces meant to defend it split between rival factions — the Saudi-backed government and the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council, which has not joined the latest fighting. More than 320,000 people have been displaced since August 1, and the World Health Organization counted 11,755 casualties in the Yemen fighting as of November 8. If the Houthis take Aden, the recognised government loses its last major stronghold in the south; if they fortify Bab al-Mandeb, the threat to Red Sea shipping — already severe — gains a permanent land base.
In short: the Houthis have closed to about 60 km of Aden after taking two Lahj districts, and are digging in along Bab al-Mandeb to threaten shipping — while the government claims counter-attacks that cannot be verified, and Aden's defenders remain divided.
Sources:
Source: nationpathindia.com.

The advance is the latest step in a ground campaign that has been moving fast since the civil war reignited this summer. The government has already pulled its last forces back from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait area to defend Aden, and the Houthis have taken over evacuated positions along more than 150 km of Red Sea coastline, from Dhubab toward Khor Amira. According to sources cited by the Institute for the Study of War, the Houthis are now building fortifications — tunnels and berms — along Bab al-Mandeb to develop a long-term ability to threaten civilian shipping in the strait at close range, exploiting the vacuum left by the government's withdrawal from all positions within 65 km of the strait. Inside Aden, the government has been digging trenches, building earth barricades and setting up checkpoints, and Yemen's parliament has unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a terrorist organisation.

The picture is not one-sided, though the claims cut both ways and neither side's battlefield reporting can be independently verified. An independent Yemeni journalist reported on Saturday that government-aligned forces assaulted and recaptured several Houthi-held positions near Am Sarih, north of Jabal Kharaz mountain in central Lahij, and retook Jabal Habanan, about 15 km north of Am Sarih — but the Institute for the Study of War says it cannot verify any of those claims. Yemen's army said on Monday it had carried out 661 attacks on Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as part of its "Dawn of Yemen" offensive launched October 5. The Houthis, for their part, say they are only hitting military and strategic targets; Riyadh calls them a terrorist militia deliberately targeting civilians.

For people in Aden, the war is now a question of distance measured in tens of kilometres, with missiles already falling on the city and the forces meant to defend it split between rival factions — the Saudi-backed government and the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council, which has not joined the latest fighting. More than 320,000 people have been displaced since August 1, and the World Health Organization counted 11,755 casualties in the Yemen fighting as of November 8. If the Houthis take Aden, the recognised government loses its last major stronghold in the south; if they fortify Bab al-Mandeb, the threat to Red Sea shipping — already severe — gains a permanent land base.

In short: the Houthis have closed to about 60 km of Aden after taking two Lahj districts, and are digging in along Bab al-Mandeb to threaten shipping — while the government claims counter-attacks that cannot be verified, and Aden's defenders remain divided.

item.title: Trump told Europe to stop funding Ukraine in an angry call after the Putin summit
item.description:
President Trump rang into a meeting of European leaders in Berlin on Thursday and told them to stop pouring billions into Ukraine, according to the Telegraph, which reported the call on Friday. Two sources described his remarks as a "tirade," saying he challenged European plans to cover Ukraine's estimated €70 billion financing gap for 2027 and argued the money could instead benefit their own "beautiful countries," as the Washington Post also reported. Trump called in from Air Force One, on Jared Kushner's phone, after his trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, and told the Europeans that Putin was tired of the war and ready to accept terms he previously would have rejected.
The call landed badly in Berlin, where leaders had gathered with President Zelenskyy to discuss emergency finance for Kyiv. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his European counterparts pushed back and reaffirmed that their support for Ukraine was unwavering. A third source offered a softer reading, saying Trump was arguing that a peace deal would save everyone money rather than ordering an end to aid — and the White House disputed the Telegraph's account, saying Trump had emphasised the war's enormous human and financial cost and that everyone should be striving for peace because it would save lives and money. Either way, no European leader publicly changed course, and the meeting went ahead with its funding plans.
The timing undercut Trump's own case. On the same day he told Europe that Putin was ready for peace, Putin publicly rejected renewed negotiations over a limited ceasefire on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping, repeated his demand that Ukraine surrender the remaining Donbas territory it controls, and rejected any European peacekeeping force in Ukraine after a settlement. Hours later, Russia launched its biggest barrage of the war on Kyiv. Trump's optimism after Shenzhen — he rated the summit "a 12" out of 10 — now sits against two nights of mass strikes, a NATO airspace violation in Poland, and a European funding debate he tried to shut down from 30,000 feet.
For Ukrainians, the stakes are immediate and financial as well as military: the €70 billion gap for 2027 is what keeps the state running and the army supplied, and the European Commission's plan to borrow up to €45 billion on capital markets to lend to Kyiv still needs approval from the European Parliament and member states. For Europeans, the call raised the question of whether Washington is still a reliable partner in funding the war at all.
In short: Trump used his post-summit call to Berlin to tell Europe to stop funding Ukraine and focus on his peace plan; the White House says he was only arguing peace would save money, the Europeans pushed back and carried on — and Putin's own words and missiles the same day contradicted the premise that he is ready to deal.

item.title: Washington's Iran decision: Netanyahu pushes a 4–7 day campaign, Trump says not before January
item.description:
President Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, the New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing US and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions — but he has not decided, and he has told reporters he will not decide until after the new year. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing hard for the United States to join a four-to-seven-day air campaign, according to the Times, backed by Israeli intelligence warnings that Iran has rebuilt the missile and drone arsenals it lost earlier in the war and is advancing chemical and biological weapons programmes as an alternative to a nuclear weapon. Mossad director Roman Gofman travelled to Washington on November 13 to press the case with senior administration officials including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Axios reported, and the Times says Trump recently told Vice President JD Vance to stop pursuing a negotiated settlement, favouring sustained economic pressure instead.
Trump's own public words point the other way on timing. Aboard Air Force One on Thursday he said, "I am not rushing into any decision [on Iran]. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," and told Israel's Channel 12 the same. In a Fox News interview in Shenzhen on Wednesday he raised the chemical and biological warning himself, saying there were indications Iran was "looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear." The New York Post reports hawks inside and outside the administration are pressing him to resume the campaign that has been paused since the summer, and the Financial Times reports the same pressure from within the administration — while Israel's ambassador to the US, Michael Leiter, told the Post that Israel believes ousting the Tehran regime "is now the only long- or even medium-term answer" and "will not hesitate to go it alone."
The pressure runs in both directions. US Central Command has warned officials about the strain the prolonged buildup is placing on American forces — "running out of time, burning money and readiness," one source told the Financial Times — and the Pentagon puts the war's cost at more than $48 billion. Gulf states have also pushed for a delay: Just The News and Fox News report Trump postponed a planned attack after appeals from the Emir of Qatar, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the UAE president, who argued for a short hold while negotiators worked toward a deal with no Iranian nuclear weapon. On Friday, Trump accused Iran of refusing to negotiate a deal acceptable to Washington, and repeated his vow that "Iran will never have a nuclear weapon ever."
The backdrop is the shipping war in the Strait of Hormuz, where two more tankers were hit on Saturday (covered in this morning's brief). The New York Post reports that since the US war with Iran began in late February, more than 120 commercial vessels have been attacked in and around the strait, killing at least 24 seafarers, according to the International Maritime Organization. More than a dozen Iranian oil tankers have gathered near Kharg Island as Tehran weighs ways to move crude despite the US naval blockade. For everyone else, the cost shows up in fuel prices and shipping insurance: Brent crude is trading around $90–92 a barrel, and every new strike keeps the risk premium in place.
In short: Israel is pushing Trump to join a four-to-seven-day air campaign against Iran, Trump says he won't decide until after the new year, and the debate is now a three-way pull — Israeli pressure, CENTCOM warning about strain, and Gulf states asking for time to negotiate — while the tanker war in the strait keeps escalating.
Sources:
Source: thebostonreport.com.

item.title: FBI's national crime database breached — again — and Trump downplays it
item.description:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), the database federal, state and local law enforcement use to share information on warrants and background checks, CNN first reported on Friday, citing two people briefed on the matter.
It is the second such breach in recent months. How the intruders got in, what they accessed and who is behind it are not public, and the FBI has not commented.
President Trump, asked about it in a Fox News phone interview on Saturday, said "it's not good — I don't like that," and used the question to revisit his grievances about the FBI's 2016 Russia investigation. CNN notes the breach comes amid a series of high-profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA's air traffic control system.

item.title: Russia hits Ukraine again overnight — a child and a paramedic killed in Zelenskyy's hometown
item.description:
Russia launched a second straight night of heavy strikes on Ukraine, hours after its biggest barrage of the war on Friday. Ukraine's Air Force said the overnight attack, which began Friday evening, involved three ballistic missiles and 148 drones, 87 of them jet-powered. Air defences shot down or jammed 117 of the drones, but impacts were recorded at 19 locations, and no ballistic-missile interceptions were reported by Saturday morning.
The deadliest strike fell on Kryvyi Rih, President Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine. Two ballistic missiles hit near a restaurant parking lot in a densely populated neighbourhood on Friday evening, and drones then struck the same area while emergency crews were responding — Ukrainian officials described the follow-up strikes as deliberately targeting rescuers and medical workers. A 7-year-old boy who had been playing near the restaurant and a 20-year-old female paramedic were killed. At least 58 people were injured, including six children, three ambulance workers and emergency responders, and the strikes set four fires and damaged around 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools, businesses and ambulances. Kyiv was hit again too: fires broke out at two private homes in the Podil district, two people were injured, and debris fell in the Solomianskyi district. In the Kharkiv region, a drone struck a five-storey residential building in Solonytsivka, injuring 11 people including two children. In Rivne region, 50 settlements lost power and an industrial facility was hit, injuring one person; a drone attack on an industrial facility in Horodnia, Chernihiv region, caused a fire but no casualties.
Russia has not commented on this specific overnight attack. Its defence ministry claimed Friday's far larger barrage — 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones — hit military and energy targets, and President Putin had vowed retaliation after Ukraine's strikes on the Kerch Bridge this week. Zelenskyy called Friday's attack "the biggest this year" and "highly demonstrative," and said Russia was using wave tactics with 20–30 minute pauses to make firefighting and repairs harder. Hours before Friday's barrage, CNN reported Trump had said a "tired" Putin was ready for a deal, after the three leaders' trilateral summit in Shenzhen billed itself as a force for peace — a summit Zelenskyy has since called a failure.
For ordinary Ukrainians, this is now two nights running of mass attacks as temperatures drop below zero: power is out in parts of Kyiv and ten other regions, three of Kyiv's Dnipro bridges were damaged on Friday, and hospitals and schools are being hit alongside energy infrastructure. Ukraine's air force says it is critically short of Patriot interceptor missiles — only three of Friday's 27 ballistic missiles were intercepted.
In short: Russia followed its record Friday barrage with another overnight wave, killing a child and a paramedic in Kryvyi Rih in what Kyiv calls a deliberate double-tap on rescuers — and the peace talk from Shenzhen has produced no pause at all.

Source: europesays.com.

The deadliest strike fell on Kryvyi Rih, President Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine. Two ballistic missiles hit near a restaurant parking lot in a densely populated neighbourhood on Friday evening, and drones then struck the same area while emergency crews were responding — Ukrainian officials described the follow-up strikes as deliberately targeting rescuers and medical workers. A 7-year-old boy who had been playing near the restaurant and a 20-year-old female paramedic were killed. At least 58 people were injured, including six children, three ambulance workers and emergency responders, and the strikes set four fires and damaged around 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools, businesses and ambulances. Kyiv was hit again too: fires broke out at two private homes in the Podil district, two people were injured, and debris fell in the Solomianskyi district. In the Kharkiv region, a drone struck a five-storey residential building in Solonytsivka, injuring 11 people including two children. In Rivne region, 50 settlements lost power and an industrial facility was hit, injuring one person; a drone attack on an industrial facility in Horodnia, Chernihiv region, caused a fire but no casualties.

Russia has not commented on this specific overnight attack. Its defence ministry claimed Friday's far larger barrage — 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones — hit military and energy targets, and President Putin had vowed retaliation after Ukraine's strikes on the Kerch Bridge this week. Zelenskyy called Friday's attack "the biggest this year" and "highly demonstrative," and said Russia was using wave tactics with 20–30 minute pauses to make firefighting and repairs harder. Hours before Friday's barrage, CNN reported Trump had said a "tired" Putin was ready for a deal, after the three leaders' trilateral summit in Shenzhen billed itself as a force for peace — a summit Zelenskyy has since called a failure.

For ordinary Ukrainians, this is now two nights running of mass attacks as temperatures drop below zero: power is out in parts of Kyiv and ten other regions, three of Kyiv's Dnipro bridges were damaged on Friday, and hospitals and schools are being hit alongside energy infrastructure. Ukraine's air force says it is critically short of Patriot interceptor missiles — only three of Friday's 27 ballistic missiles were intercepted.

In short: Russia followed its record Friday barrage with another overnight wave, killing a child and a paramedic in Kryvyi Rih in what Kyiv calls a deliberate double-tap on rescuers — and the peace talk from Shenzhen has produced no pause at all.

item.title: Rutte in Warsaw: NATO will defend "every inch" of Poland after Russian missiles land
item.description:
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte visited Warsaw on Saturday, a day after Poland said Russia violated its airspace with three objects — probably two missiles and a drone — during the massive strikes on Ukraine. "I can guarantee that NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory," Rutte said, according to Polish Press Agency PAP. He added that the head of NATO forces in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, would do everything necessary to identify threats and make appropriate adjustments to defence and deterrence.
The response is now moving into formal channels. A meeting of NATO's North Atlantic Council will be held in Brussels on Monday to discuss the violation, PAP reported, and France's foreign minister has called for a UN Security Council meeting. Poland is formally asking NATO for more troops and surveillance aircraft for Operation Eastern Sentry, the mission guarding the alliance's eastern flank, and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz has specifically asked allies to deploy additional AWACS aircraft and F-35 jets to Poland. The Institute for the Study of War assesses the Kremlin conducted the violations deliberately, to coincide with the Coalition of the Willing military exercise at Nowa Dęba — one Kh-101 cruise missile crashed about 35 km from the exercise site, and Polish officials say the timing was no coincidence. Polish forces tracked as many as 11 missiles and drones that could have threatened Polish airspace; three crossed it. No one was hurt and nothing was damaged in Poland, and Moscow has not commented.
Warsaw calls it an intentional provocation; the UK's defence intelligence chief, Lt Gen Matthew Jones, said he is confident Russia "does not actively seek war with NATO" but warned the greatest fear is "a significant miscalculation." That split — deliberate provocation versus a miscalculation risk — is the argument inside the alliance now: Poland and the Baltic states want a harder posture and more hardware on the eastern flank, while the assessment from London is that Moscow is testing responses, not starting a war with NATO.
For people in southeastern Poland, Friday meant air-raid alerts on their phones, Rzeszów airport suspending operations, rail halted for about an hour in the Subcarpathian region, and Patriots activated around Rzeszów-Jasionka and Świdnik. The Coalition of the Willing exercise continues near the crash sites, and Rutte's visit is meant as a visible guarantee that the alliance will answer the next incursion the same way.
In short: NATO's chief flew to Warsaw to promise Poland's defence in person, a formal alliance meeting is set for Monday, and Poland wants more troops and jets — while the open question is whether Moscow was deliberately probing NATO or risking an accident.

item.title: Two more tankers hit near Hormuz as hawks push Trump to resume Iran strikes
item.description:
Two tankers were hit by unknown projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, the latest in a run of attacks on commercial shipping that has now stretched for weeks. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) said one outbound tanker was struck on the stern about 11 nautical miles north of Oman's Khasab, and a second was hit in its engine room 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. It was not immediately clear whether the two reports involved the same vessel. No casualties were reported in either incident. Iran's navy said separately on Saturday that an oil tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait — Reuters could not independently verify that account or establish whether it referred to either UKMTO incident. A tanker hit near Khasab on Friday also caught fire, with no casualties reported.
The attacks come as pressure builds in Washington to resume major strikes on Iran. The New York Post reports that hawks inside and outside the administration are pressing President Trump to renew the campaign that has been on pause since the summer, and the Financial Times reported that administration hawks are pushing the same way. At the same time, more than a dozen Iranian oil tankers have reportedly gathered near Kharg Island, Iran's main oil-export terminal, as Tehran weighs ways to move crude despite the US naval blockade — Iran's state-affiliated Fars News Agency has floated the idea of a tanker convoy through the Gulf of Oman. Trump said this week he is "not rushing" decisions on Iran and to "see what happens after the new year starts," and the Senate voted on Thursday against a resolution to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran.
Tehran says it is enforcing restrictions on vessels passing through the strait and has attacked ships it says violated them, as it tries to assert control over the waterway and pressure Washington. The US and its partners treat the strikes as attacks on commercial shipping. Around 18–20 vessels have now been hit this month, and shipping through the strait is running well below pre-war levels, with more than half of Gulf tankers now using ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman to keep oil moving.
For everyone else, the cost shows up at the pump and in supply chains: Brent crude is trading around $90–92 a barrel, and the strait carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil. Every new strike raises insurance and shipping costs and keeps the risk premium in fuel prices, even as flows continue.
In short: two more tankers were hit near Hormuz on Saturday, Iran claims one of them hit a mine, and the attacks are now fuelling a debate in Washington over whether to resume strikes on Iran — while Tehran masses tankers to test the blockade.

Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Aden braces as Houthis close in — and Riyadh takes another missile salvo
item.description:
Yemen's war is closing in on Aden, the temporary capital of the internationally recognised government, and the forces meant to defend it are divided. Reuters reported from the city on Friday that the Houthis are now only about 80 km (50 miles) away on the front line in the highlands to the north, and 110 km to the west along a desert road with few natural obstacles. Inside Aden, soldiers have set up checkpoints, pulled in reinforcements, dug trenches and built earth barricades on roads toward the front — but feuding among rival factions, and between their Gulf backers, is undermining the defence. The Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the UAE, has not taken part in the latest fighting against the Houthis, though it says it will defend Aden and the south if needed. "These forces may share a common enemy in the Houthis, but they do not share the same political objectives, territorial priorities, or willingness to fight," Yemen analyst Mohammed al-Basha of the Royal United Services Institute told Reuters.
The Houthis have been advancing on nearly every front since the civil war reignited this summer after a four-year truce, and they have already hit Aden itself with missile and drone strikes — including, the Houthis claim, ballistic missiles at a Saudi coalition command centre in the al-Buraiqa district, where the government is based. The Saudi-led coalition has been bombing Houthi targets in return, striking Hodeidah port and missile and drone facilities around Sanaa on Friday. Early on Saturday, the coalition said it intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh — the second attack on the Saudi capital in two days after Thursday's strike damaged the PIF Tower, the country's tallest skyscraper. Saudi civil defence issued an aerial-threat alert at 1:53 a.m., residents heard two explosions, and the all-clear followed; no casualties or damage were reported. The Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh, and also accused the coalition of striking a civilian boat in Yemeni waters, killing more than a dozen people — that claim is unverified and comes from a single source.
Riyadh says the Houthis are a terrorist militia deliberately targeting civilians and airports; the Houthis say they only hit military and strategic targets, and deny Saudi claims that they have targeted the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The World Health Organization counted 11,755 casualties in the Yemen fighting as of November 8 — 2,098 killed and 9,657 wounded — and more than 320,000 people have been displaced since August 1.
For people in Aden, the choice is bleak: stay in a city now being hit by missiles, or leave for an impoverished countryside. Residents told Reuters they lie awake listening for blasts, in a city where state salaries barely cover living expenses, and hundreds of thousands of displaced people are already surviving on meagre aid in small tarpaulin camps in the hills.
In short: the Houthis are within 80 km of Aden, the government's defenders are split between rival factions, and the missile war with Saudi Arabia is escalating in parallel — with Riyadh hit twice in two days and the coalition bombing Houthi ports and Sanaa in return.

item.title: Houthis fire three ballistic missiles at Riyadh — the second attack on the Saudi capital in two days
item.description:
The Saudi-led coalition said early Saturday it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthis toward Riyadh, the second Houthi attack on the Saudi capital in as many days, after Thursday's strike damaged the Public Investment Fund tower, the kingdom's tallest skyscraper. A Reuters witness in Riyadh saw a projectile streak across the sky shortly before hearing a loud bang, leaving a trail of smoke. No casualties or damage from the Saturday attack have been reported.
According to Reuters, the coalition said its air defences intercepted the three missiles, while the Houthis threatened to target Saudi Red Sea ports, warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, and claimed attacks on a power station and a port in southern Saudi Arabia. The attack followed an escalation on Friday, when the coalition said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah and carried out operations targeting Houthi missile and drone capabilities in the capital Sanaa. Al Arabiya and Al Jazeera also reported the coalition's statement that the three missiles aimed at Riyadh had been intercepted. It comes a day after Friday evening's separate Houthi attack on the southern Jazan province, where two ballistic missiles were intercepted, and Thursday's strike on the PIF tower, which blew out windows across seven or eight floors of the 80-storey building.
The two sides are locked in a widening exchange with no sign of slowing. The Houthis have vowed continued strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities, and have extended evacuation warnings to shipping companies; their stated aim is to pressure Riyadh over the Yemen war, where Saudi-backed government forces have fallen back to defend Aden while the Houthis sit roughly 100 km west of the city. Riyadh, for its part, has stepped up retaliatory strikes on Sanaa and Hodeidah, and Reuters reported this week that Saudi planners expect the Yemen campaign to last up to six months into 2027, with the goal of gaining territory before any negotiations. The United States has so far withheld offensive support — intelligence, precision munitions and targeting help — which Saudi officials say could compress the campaign to weeks if provided, though Washington has sent more than 100 intelligence advisers under a joint command.
For people in Riyadh, the war is now arriving over the capital twice in two days: air-raid alerts, explosions heard in the city, and warnings to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace. item.description:

item.title: Nvidia craters 14% as the SEC opens an accounting probe — and the AI selloff spreads
item.description:
Nvidia's stock fell 14% on Friday after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is probing the company's accounting practices, capping a week in which the chipmaker lost nearly 23% of its value and more than 47% from its early-October peak. It was the seventh straight weekly decline — a stretch not seen since July 2008 — and the seventh straight losing session, over which Nvidia has shed roughly $1.16 trillion in market value. Shares touched a 52-week low of $126.64 during the session, and the company's market cap now sits at about $3.03 trillion, below Google parent Alphabet's $3.24 trillion — making Nvidia the fourth-largest U.S. company, behind Alphabet for the first time since April 2024.
According to MarketWatch, the SEC probe was reported by Reuters on Friday afternoon and centers on potential accounting issues, with renewed scrutiny of Nvidia's Singapore revenue reporting. The same day, the New York Times reported that Alice Huang — the former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed with whom Jensen Huang previously admitted an extramarital affair, and who U.S. officials suspect was a Chinese intelligence asset — has ties through "family and associates" to China's defense industry. The board's investigation into whether Huang compromised national security or revealed corporate secrets is the backdrop to all of it: Huang resigned as CEO on November 12, CFO Colette Kress is interim chief, the board says it does not intend to reinstate him, and the search firm Heidrick & Struggles has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas about the permanent job, Bloomberg reported. President Donald Trump weighed in at a Friday news conference, saying he would "like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back" to Nvidia, adding: "We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them."
The two sides of the market argument are now starkly split. On one side, Nvidia's business itself just delivered blockbuster numbers — $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue on Tuesday, up 103% year over year, with $130 billion in fourth-quarter guidance, both above expectations — and some analysts think the selling is overdone: Seaport Research's Jay Goldberg told MarketWatch he expects things to stabilize next week, though "there is no one in a hurry to buy it until we know who the next CEO is." On the other side, fund managers who held Nvidia as a "safety stock" are rotating out, Goldberg said, and Catalyst Funds' David Miller called the stock "vulnerable" to more selling, saying the length of the losing streak "tells us very little about where the bottom is" and that he would want "greater clarity on permanent leadership and the investigations, along with continued execution on customer demand and product deliveries, before becoming confident in a sustained recovery." MarketWatch also notes the stock was already under pressure before Huang's exit, with investors questioning whether AI demand can sustain current spending.
The damage spread well beyond Nvidia on Friday. Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq only the day before, fell 8.5% to close at $88.91 — after touching $83.05 intraday, just five cents above its $83 IPO price — giving back most of its 17% first-day gain. The Nasdaq tumbled 5.3% on Friday and 10% for the week, its biggest five-day percentage decline since March 2020 and its worst points decline on record, while AMD fell 11% to $433.50. For ordinary investors, the stakes are direct: Nvidia made up 6.14% of the largest S&P 500 index fund as of November 12, so the slide is hitting retirement accounts and index portfolios, not just traders — and the same AI-valuation doubts dragging Nvidia down are now washing over the whole sector, including a stock that raised a record $81 billion barely 24 hours earlier.
In short: a reported SEC accounting probe turned Nvidia's bad week into a rout — down 14% Friday, down 23% on the week, at a 52-week low and below Alphabet in market value — while Trump publicly urged Huang to apologize and return, the CEO search drags on, and the AI selloff pulled Anthropic and the Nasdaq down with it. Watch for Huang's transcribed interview before three House committees on December 1, any formal SEC statement, and whether a permanent CEO is named.
*Sources: MarketWatch, Reuters via Blockchain Academics, Vocemundi, CNN, The Times, Barron's*
Source: marketwatch.com.

item.title: Poland asks NATO for reinforcements after Russian missiles cross its border — and NATO's chief calls it a "grave violation"
item.description:
Poland will formally ask NATO for more troops and surveillance aircraft for the alliance's eastern flank after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crossed into its airspace during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine, Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the incursion a "grave violation" of Polish airspace, said he had spoken with Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and is expected to travel to Poland this weekend. Warsaw also plans to seek an extraordinary meeting of NATO member states.
According to the Associated Press, one missile — identified as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile — came down at Nowy Lipowiec, about 50 km from the Ukrainian border and roughly 35 km from where European troops were conducting exercises; a second likely missile fell at Rudnik nad Sanem, and the probable jet-powered drone at Mołodycz. Poland's military said 11 objects threatened its airspace and three crossed, all travelling faster than 800 km/h. The Kh-101 spent about three minutes over Poland. Polish F-16s and Swedish Gripen fighters were airborne, Patriot batteries were activated around Rzeszów-Jasionka airport and Świdnik, and two NATO AWACS aircraft were operating over Poland — but nobody fired: a Swedish pilot could not get visual identification in poor weather, and the firing chain could not positively identify the fast-moving tracks in the time available. Rzeszów airport suspended operations and rail traffic was halted in the Subcarpathian region for about an hour. Nobody in Poland was hurt and no infrastructure was destroyed, and Moscow has not commented.
The two sides are reading the incident in opposite ways. Tusk called it an "intentional provocation," saying "we know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia" and that it "does not look like an accident" — and pointed to the timing: the incursions happened while thousands of troops from 11 European countries were taking part in the KOALICJA 26.2 exercise in southeastern Poland, rehearsing a possible postwar stabilization mission in Ukraine. Russia has said nothing about the Polish incident, but on Friday Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said even a quasi-NATO membership for Ukraine would be unacceptable, and Putin has said European troops deployed to Ukraine after a peace deal would be legitimate targets. European leaders condemned the incursion — Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it "utterly unacceptable," European Council President António Costa said Russia "continues to spread (its) threats" — while the UK's chief of defence intelligence, Lt. Gen. Matthew Jones, said he was confident Russia "does not actively seek war with NATO," but that his greatest fear "is the risk of a significant miscalculation," warning there have been "too many recent examples of reckless Russian behavior where, if the incident had been slightly different, the results could have been extremely serious."
For people in southeastern Poland, the war is no longer something across the border: alarms sounded in border towns after 6:30 a.m., an airport shut down, trains stopped, and explosive-ordnance teams were deployed to villages where missile fragments fell in fields and forests. It is the second Russian missile to come down in Biłgoraj County in under four months, and the episode forced NATO pilots to make a shoot-or-hold decision in about three minutes, in bad weather, against objects they could not positively identify — exactly the kind of split-second judgment where a mistake could kill civilians or trigger a wider war.
In short: Poland is treating Friday's incursion as a deliberate Russian probe timed to NATO exercises, and is asking the alliance for more forces and surveillance — while NATO's chief calls it a grave violation and heads to Warsaw, and allied commanders warn the real danger is miscalculation, not intent. Watch for Rutte's visit this weekend, whether NATO agrees to reinforce Operation Eastern Sentry, and whether Poland invokes Article 4 consultations.

Poland will formally ask NATO for more troops and surveillance aircraft for the alliance's eastern flank after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crossed into its airspace during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine, Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the incursion a "grave violation" of Polish airspace, said he had spoken with Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and is expected to travel to Poland this weekend. Warsaw also plans to seek an extraordinary meeting of NATO member states.

According to the Associated Press, one missile — identified as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile — came down at Nowy Lipowiec, about 50 km from the Ukrainian border and roughly 35 km from where European troops were conducting exercises; a second likely missile fell at Rudnik nad Sanem, and the probable jet-powered drone at Mołodycz. Poland's military said 11 objects threatened its airspace and three crossed, all travelling faster than 800 km/h. The Kh-101 spent about three minutes over Poland. Polish F-16s and Swedish Gripen fighters were airborne, Patriot batteries were activated around Rzeszów-Jasionka airport and Świdnik, and two NATO AWACS aircraft were operating over Poland — but nobody fired: a Swedish pilot could not get visual identification in poor weather, and the firing chain could not positively identify the fast-moving tracks in the time available. Rzeszów airport suspended operations and rail traffic was halted in the Subcarpathian region for about an hour. Nobody in Poland was hurt and no infrastructure was destroyed, and Moscow has not commented.

The two sides are reading the incident in opposite ways. Tusk called it an "intentional provocation," saying "we know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia" and that it "does not look like an accident" — and pointed to the timing: the incursions happened while thousands of troops from 11 European countries were taking part in the KOALICJA 26.2 exercise in southeastern Poland, rehearsing a possible postwar stabilization mission in Ukraine. Russia has said nothing about the Polish incident, but on Friday Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said even a quasi-NATO membership for Ukraine would be unacceptable, and Putin has said European troops deployed to Ukraine after a peace deal would be legitimate targets. European leaders condemned the incursion — Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it "utterly unacceptable," European Council President António Costa said Russia "continues to spread (its) threats" — while the UK's chief of defence intelligence, Lt. Gen. Matthew Jones, said he was confident Russia "does not actively seek war with NATO," but that his greatest fear "is the risk of a significant miscalculation," warning there have been "too many recent examples of reckless Russian behavior where, if the incident had been slightly different, the results could have been extremely serious."

For people in southeastern Poland, the war is no longer something across the border: alarms sounded in border towns after 6:30 a.m., an airport shut down, trains stopped, and explosive-ordnance teams were deployed to villages where missile fragments fell in fields and forests. It is the second Russian missile to come down in Biłgoraj County in under four months, and the episode forced NATO pilots to make a shoot-or-hold decision in about three minutes, in bad weather, against objects they could not positively identify — exactly the kind of split-second judgment where a mistake could kill civilians or trigger a wider war.

In short: Poland is treating Friday's incursion as a deliberate Russian probe timed to NATO exercises, and is asking the alliance for more forces and surveillance — while NATO's chief calls it a grave violation and heads to Warsaw, and allied commanders warn the real danger is miscalculation, not intent. Watch for Rutte's visit this weekend, whether NATO agrees to reinforce Operation Eastern Sentry, and whether Poland invokes Article 4 consultations.

item.title: Judge refuses to dismiss Alex Murdaugh's murder indictments — retrial stays on for April 2027
item.description:
A South Carolina judge on Friday refused to dismiss the original murder indictments against Alex Murdaugh, clearing the way for his retrial in the 2021 killings of his wife and son. Judge Debra McCaslin issued an 11-page order denying Murdaugh's motion to dismiss the murder and weapons charges, after hearing nearly two hours of arguments at a pretrial hearing in Lexington on November 13. The retrial is now set to begin the week of April 5, 2027, in Sumter County, before McCaslin.
Murdaugh's defense argued that the lead state investigator, South Carolina Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen, gave false or misleading testimony to a Colleton County grand jury in 2022 in order to secure the indictments — specifically about human blood spatter on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings, and about shotgun ammunition patterns matching one of the missing murder weapons. Prosecutors countered that the remaining evidence established probable cause regardless, and said they were prepared to seek a fresh set of indictments as soon as next month if the defense had succeeded. McCaslin sided with the state: she wrote that Murdaugh "has not established intentional prosecutorial or investigative misconduct that compromised the integrity of the grand jury proceedings," and that "the remaining unchallenged evidence overwhelmingly established probable cause." She added that dismissal of an indictment over alleged grand-jury misconduct is "an extraordinary remedy reserved for exceptional circumstances."
The ruling lands in a case that has already been through one full trial and a reversal. Murdaugh was convicted of both murders in 2023 and sentenced to life, but the South Carolina Supreme Court overturned the convictions earlier this year, citing "shocking jury interference" by the court clerk in the Colleton County trial. The defense's strategy at the retrial has been to attack the investigation itself — including claims that officers mishandled the murder weapons — while prosecutors have fought to keep the original indictments and the evidence behind them intact. The next milestone is January 20, 2027, the deadline for both sides to agree on a juror questionnaire to be mailed to potential Sumter County jurors.
For the families, the ruling means the case finally has a firm path forward after months of pretrial fights over DNA testing, ballistics data and the grand jury record — but also that the retrial, now more than five years after Maggie and Paul Murdaugh were killed at the family's Moselle property, is still nearly five months away.
In short: Judge McCaslin found the alleged grand-jury errors did not amount to bad-faith misconduct and did not undercut probable cause, so the original murder indictments stand and the April 5, 2027 retrial in Sumter County goes ahead. Watch for the January 20 juror-questionnaire deadline and any further pretrial rulings on evidence.
*Sources: AP via Reflector, Greenville Online, Fox News, MyTV Charleston*

item.title: Apple is reportedly building its own autonomous AI agent — from job listings, not an announcement
item.description:
Apple has posted job listings this week for engineers to build an autonomous AI agent that can browse the web, use apps, run commands, write and fix code, and control devices on a user's behalf, Bloomberg reported on November 19. One listing, for a "Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive," says Apple is building agents that work the way people do — moving between a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor and a service — with permission models and sandboxing as design priorities. The project is in its early stages and could launch as early as late 2027, though Apple has not confirmed a timeline. This is a report based on hiring, not an Apple announcement — treat it as an early signal, not a product. The same week, Apple seeded second public betas of iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3, which make it harder for third-party agents to get control of a Mac.
*Sources: MacDailyNews (Bloomberg), TipRanks*

item.title: Russia's promised retaliation hits Kyiv's bridges — and spills into Poland
item.description:
Russia launched one of the largest missile and drone attacks of the war overnight, hours after Vladimir Putin vowed a response "far more painful" than Ukraine's repeated strikes on the Kerch Bridge. Eight people were killed across Ukraine and 28 injured, and for the first time in the war Russia hit three of Kyiv's bridges across the Dnipro River — the biggest strikes yet on the routes connecting the two halves of the capital. The same barrage also violated Polish airspace, with three objects — likely two missiles and a drone, according to Poland's defence minister — crossing the border and falling in southeastern Poland.
According to Reuters, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic, targeting energy, logistics and railway infrastructure across the country. Ukraine's Air Force put the count at 84 cruise missiles plus Iskander-M and S-400 ballistic missiles and Zircon hypersonic missiles, and 404 drones including 123 jet-powered Shaheds — and said air defences downed or suppressed 462 weapons in total. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said six people were killed in Kyiv and 15 injured, with two more killed at a railway station in Lviv. In Kyiv, missiles hit the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges, forcing closures and weight limits; a water utility facility was hit, killing three employees and dropping water pressure in four districts, and five districts lost power. In Kharkiv, Russian drones hit an emergency hospital, wounding four and damaging its MRI unit. Power outages were reported in ten regions, and emergency cuts were introduced in the west. The attack also spilled over the border: Poland scrambled jets, and its army is investigating reports of objects falling near the village of Chmielek, about 45 km from the Ukrainian border. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there was currently no air threat, while the defence minister denounced the incursion as a Russian "provocation" and Britain's prime minister condemned it.
The two sides are arguing from opposite ends of the same logic. Kyiv says its bridge and refinery strikes are retaliation for Russia's nightly campaign against Ukrainian power plants and cities, and that they will continue until Russia stops hitting Ukrainian infrastructure — Zelenskyy called the overnight attack "highly demonstrative" terror meant to compensate for Russia's "military and diplomatic impotence," and said Putin's attempt to "redraw the world" with Trump and Xi at Thursday's Shenzhen summit had been a "failure." Moscow calls the Kerch Bridge civilian infrastructure — even as it is a key supply route for Russian forces in occupied Crimea — while its own energy strikes on Ukraine continue; Russia's Defence Ministry said it struck plants and warehouses linked to Ukrainian missile and drone production, plus power, transport and port facilities. Washington and its European allies are split on the diplomacy: Trump embraced Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, where the three leaders signed a four-point "declaration of peace" that did not mention Ukraine or Iran; European leaders in Berlin warned on Thursday against any attempt to decide a peace settlement over Ukraine's head, and after the summit Zelenskyy and European leaders issued a joint statement urging Russia to accept a ceasefire covering energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping corridors — which Putin has now rejected.
For people on the ground, the war has removed the idea of a safe hour. Thursday's daytime drone attack on Kyiv killed a 26-year-old man, injured five others, and damaged two European embassies and St. Volodymyr's Cathedral; the overnight barrage then hit homes, a hospital and a water plant while much of Kyiv is already living on around four hours of electricity a day. In the capital, over a third of the city's 3 million residents live on the eastern bank of the Dnipro but most work on the western bank, so damaged bridges mean disrupted commutes for hundreds of thousands of people. In Crimea, the bridge's rail link remains disrupted, with ferries due to start running from Friday as the fallback.
In short: Putin's promised retaliation arrived within hours of his Shenzhen warning, in the form of a multi-wave missile attack that killed eight people, knocked out power across ten regions, hit three Kyiv bridges for the first time, and spilled into Polish airspace — while the diplomacy meant to stop it produced a declaration that said nothing about Ukraine at all. Watch for whether Russia keeps striking into Friday night, how Poland and NATO respond to the airspace violation, and whether the energy-infrastructure ceasefire idea survives the weekend.
*Sources: Reuters via SRN News, AP via EuropeSays, The Times, Kyiv City Military Administration via h.ua, Reuters on Poland*
Source: srnnews.com.

item.title: This one is a catch-up: the verdict and sentencing happened on November 5 and 9, but they were never reported in these briefs, which kept saying the trial had "no fresh developments."
item.description:
Russell Brand was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on Monday, November 9, to 10 years and six months in prison after a jury convicted him of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
The jury, which deliberated for eight and a half hours after a four-week trial that began October 12, convicted the 51-year-old comedian on four of seven charges — raping a woman who had attended one of his comedy shows in 2009, and sexually assaulting three other women between 2004 and 2009 — and cleared him of two further rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault. Judge Joel Bennathan, passing sentence, described Brand as a "sexual predator" with a "staggering arrogance" and a "casual, arrogant disregard of any woman's right to say no to you." He handed down nine years for the rape, plus nine months, 18 months and eight months for the three sexual assaults, served consecutively to the rape sentence for a total of ten years and six months. Under UK rules Brand must serve two-thirds — about seven years — before he can be released on licence. He showed no emotion as the sentence was delivered, according to the Press Association, and had spent the four nights since the verdict on remand at HMP Wandsworth.
The two sides' positions were starkly different throughout. Prosecutors presented Brand as a "ruthless, calculated and manipulative" predator who used his fame to prey on women; Brand denied all charges, told the court "I am innocent," and said he never had sex without consent. His wife Laura gave evidence calling him a "wonderful father" and an "amazing" husband. The case followed a joint 2023 investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4's *Dispatches* that prompted women to come forward. Brand's father Ron disputed the verdict outside court after sentencing. Police have also said Brand is being investigated over two further rape allegations from other women.
For the women involved, the verdict closes a case that began with allegations from more than two decades ago — one complainant read her victim impact statement in person at the sentencing hearing. Brand can still appeal: the window for appealing the conviction runs 28 days from November 5, and for the sentence from November 9. No appeal had been announced as of this morning.
In short: after a trial the briefs wrongly treated as quiet, Russell Brand was convicted on November 5 of one rape and three sexual assaults and sentenced on November 9 to ten and a half years in prison — the biggest court outcome of the month, and one this watch missed until now.
*Sources: CNN, The Times, Wall Street Journal, People*
Source: cnn.com.
